claims.text: The starting material is nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 produced by powder metallurgy.
The starting W38Ta36Cr15V11 material has a homogeneous microstructure.
Unmodified nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 exhibits radiation-induced precipitation at approximately 8 dpa.
Unmodified nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 exhibits negligible irradiation hardening at approximately 8 dpa.
Approximately 1 at.% carbon added during synthesis will suppress radiation-induced precipitation in W38Ta36Cr15V11.
Carbon will bind with Cr and V at irradiation-induced defect sites.
Carbon-stabilized Cr/V complexes or short-range clusters will form at irradiation-induced defects.
The carbon-stabilized complexes will act as defect sinks.
Irradiation-generated vacancies and mobile interstitials can enhance precipitation nucleation kinetics.
Carbon will segregate to irradiation defects and interfaces and react preferentially with Cr and V.
Stable C-(Cr,V) complexes will limit Cr and V diffusion and clustering.
Carbon complex formation will reduce the thermodynamic driving force for Cr/V precipitation.
Thermodynamic instability can drive irradiation-induced precipitation in compositionally unstable alloys.
Carbon will enhance interface bonding during consolidation.
At approximately 8 dpa and 600-700 °C, carbon doping will reduce the volume fraction of Cr/V-rich precipitates by approximately 50% relative to the unmodified alloy.
The carbon-doped alloy will retain irradiation-induced hardness changes within 5%.
The carbon-doped alloy will show better densification and grain connectivity after sintering than the unmodified alloy.

Elemental powder mixing followed by spark plasma sintering can consolidate high-entropy-alloy powders into fine-grained, high-density material suitable for high-temperature and plasma-facing applications.
The carbon intervention is applicable up to approximately 8 dpa and between 600 and 700 °C.
Poorly distributed or excessive carbon may produce unwanted carbide phases and adversely affect mechanical properties.
